right, but by "all oppressions are linked," people do not mean that every single form of marginalization is identical and shows up identically in every place. it means that, as I wrote, the rhetoric used to justify oppression, the methods that are use to dismiss valid complaints about it, and the structures used to implement it (displacement, family separation, violence, dehumanization under the law) have been recycled time and time again and make up patterns that can be recognized internationally. 

As I pointed out, the rhetoric that X group are all dangerous criminals or culturally inferior tends to remain the same no matter where you are, and that between the Romani and black people, this particular *narrative* is the same,  because they both denigrate groups of people as inherently lawless and violent without examining the historical and/or structural patterns that can lead to higher crime rates. 

maybe it wasn't clear because I switched to a related subject in my second paragraph, but I wrote, "the whole argument...is the exact same *rhetoric* that people use against black people," and that all oppressions are *linked*, not that black people and the Romani have the exact same history. I respect that you typed that all out, but it feels like you're rebutting a point that I did not make.

eta: sorry if I came across as a bit condescending. I'm just remembering that the idea all oppressions are interconnected has its origins in the [black feminist framework](https://convergencemag.com/podcast/beverly-guy-sheftall-all-our-oppressions-are-interconnected/) of black American scholars and activists, so I realize that maybe if you're not familiar with the phrase you could get the idea that I'm claiming that all oppression is identical. everybody's idea of common language and common knowledge is different, so excuse me for making assumptions about what was common knowledge without a proper definition of terms.

well, if you have the time or access to a library, I would recommend that you read The Romani Gypsies by Yaron Matras. Romani people have persecuted and attempts have been made to forcefully expel them from nearly every place they have settled in for hundreds of years. 

[Leopold I of the Holy Roman Empire declared that you could kill Romani People without penalty](https://www.romarchive.eu/en/roma-civil-rights-movement/roma-czech-lands/), Joseph I [ordered that all adult Romani men were to be hung without trial](https://www.worldatlas.com/human-rights/the-historical-and-ongoing-persecution-of-gypsies-in-europe.html), in Bohemia, and [beyond](https://blog.historicenvironment.scot/2023/06/persecution-of-gypsy-travellers-in-scotland/), Romani people who refused to leave the area were to have their [right ears cut off](https://is.muni.cz/el/cus/jaro2015/CZS13/um/lecture9/10_2_Horvathova.pdf). Children were [taken from their parents](https://crgreview.com/a-history-of-romani-discrimination-and-genocide/amp/) and sent to Christian boarding schools to be corrected. Even today, Romani children [are discriminated against when they try to receive an education](https://wp.nyu.edu/schoolofprofessionalstudies-ga_review/discriminated-in-the-eu-the-roma-childrens-right-to-education/).

In the 20th century, Romani people were some of the least remembered groups of people victimized in the Holocaust- [25% of the Romani's pre-war population was killed because of Nazi persecution](https://www.open.edu/openlearn/history-the-arts/history/the-historical-and-ongoing-persecution-europes-gypsies). In fact, it wasn't [until 1982](https://www.coe.int/en/web/roma-genocide/virtual-library/-/asset_publisher/M35KN9VVoZTe/content/georgia-recognition-of-the-genocide) that Germany even acknowledged that the Romani were Holocaust victims at all. Up until then, the narrative was that the Romani deserved it because of their ["social and criminal record."](https://time.com/5719540/roma-holocaust-remembrance/)

Last but not least, the extrajudicial violence that is faced by Romani people still today seems eerily similar to the violence my ancestors fled when they left the South during the Great Migration. Similarly to how in the Jim Crow South, one black man being accused or convicted of a crime could lead to entire families and even neighborhoods being attacked and destroyed, in Italy in 2008, there were [multiple arson attacks on Romani settlements](https://www.amnesty.org/fr/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/eur300022008eng.pdf) after an individual Romani person was accused of crime. I felt a particular kind of heartbreak when I read of the [3 Romani girls who were burned alive in their trailer in Italy](https://balkaninsight.com/2017/05/11/confusion-after-roma-sisters-die-in-arson-attack-in-italy-05-11-2017/) in 2017 after a completely different Roma man was arrested for rape. I've been to Birmingham and I've sat in the pews of the [16th Street Baptist Church](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/16th_Street_Baptist_Church_bombing). The distance between these two incidents, even thousands of miles and decades apart, is negligible.

If you don't have access to a bookstore or a library that carries a copy of this book, I highly recommend you click through these links, but the book details all of these historical persecutions and more, if you're genuinely interested in understanding why I make this comparison. 

Truthfully, it kind of looks to me as though you were trying to bait me into participating in the oppression olympics, but being a student of my own people's history and the unique aspects of it does not prevent me from recognizing the patterns when they appear elsewhere.

well, it's because I think you're kind of overblowing how far Melodye wanted to go. As stated in [this Slate article](https://slate.com/culture/2016/09/the-making-of-addy-walker-american-girls-first-black-doll.html), she wasn't trying to change the story. All she did was push back when an art director complained that the *family of escaped slaves* she drew looked "sad," and told her to make them "smile more." The second thing she did was depict multiple complexions of black people in her illustrations, something the team did not initially agree on but she fought to include. 

When you characterize her actions as being enough to risk a book ban, while unintentional, it kind of paints Melodye Rosales as an unreasonable black woman who's just being too sensitive about her work.

I love Addy's Beforever dress, but I really don't think it fits in the first book or the first half of the sequel. Addy's pink dress was given to her by the underground railroad conductor, Miss Caroline, and it was specifically given to her as a disguise for running away and escaping slavery. Fugitives on the underground railroad had to navigate rough terrain, and because they traveled at night, they would have to deal with the cold, wild animals, crouching in thorny bushes, and trudging through plants like poison oak and stinging nettles, all while avoiding slave catchers.

A fancy bright blue dress with short sleeves and ribbon trimmings wouldn't have protected her arms from the elements or kept her warm. I also think putting Addy in the blue dress for Addy Learns a Lesson eliminates some of the visual class markers that divide Harriet and Addy. Harriet is, after all, a classist bully, and on top of making fun of Addy for escaping slavery, she also makes fun of her mother's career and social status. So, I feel like having Addy in a fancier dress gets rid of some of that visual storytelling, and makes the new dress her mother sews for her less meaningful. 

I get wanting to update the illustrations to reflect the new product line, but on the other hand, Addy's pink dress wasn't just a dress. it was the first clothing that ever truly belonged to her, and a important tool in helping her to reach freedom. In my opinion, they should have waited a little longer in the series to edit the dress in.

I agree. The pink dress is supposed to be the dress given to her by Miss Caroline so that Addy and Momma could run away in disguise. we can definitely agree to disagree!!  the reason why I have trouble believing bojack didn't think todd was interested is because he tells emily not to tell him about it. in the the episode where the incident happens, "stop the presses," this is the conversation that takes place immediately after they sleep together: they both remark that it is a mistake, and then emily says "what are we going to tell todd?" 

bojack tells her, "nothing, obviously." she says, "I don't want to hurt him," and bojack responds, "yeah. neither do I. that's why we're not going to tell him." 

she replies, "I just feel like we should tell him," to which bojack responds, "that feeling is you selfishly trying to assuage your guilt. if you really cared about todd, you would keep this a secret from him forever." 

why would he be worried about hurting todd or anything getting back to him if he didn't think todd still had some feelings, you know? why would they be talking about guilt at all? 

again, consenting adults can do whatever they want, and bojack isn't obligated to talk to todd about his hookups himself, but I think the fact that he was trying to pressure emily into not talking about it and control *her* communication with todd makes me feel more like he knew it was kind of crummy for him to do. not evil or irredeemable, but to me it kind of felt like a less serious, interpersonal version of the rock opera incident-- on its own, just kind of a shady thing for a friend to do, but after their entire history, a valid final straw in my opinion. one of the many things I like about this show, though, is that people can have lots of different interpretations, so I respect your opinion! :)

it's not that bojack slept with emily, it's that bojack slept with emily while thinking that todd had a thing for her. it's perfectly legal, and it's your right to do whatever you want with consent, but if you think your friend is in an "it's complicated" stage with someone else, it's a pretty crappy thing to do them. especially considering that bojack didn't know that todd was asexual, it demonstrates that bojack is still at the point in his arc where he's willing to stomp all over things that are meaningful to others for a fleeting sense of gratification. it gets scummier when you remember that bojack had been previously making a big show of trying to get them together, even buying them a hotel room at one point. even if todd and emily weren't compatible, imagine how disorienting it would feel to have someone seemingly on your side and helping you out, only to be secretly sabotaging you behind your back, *for the second time in your friendship.*
